subject: chemistry

items.q: In the chemical sense of the word, which of these samples is pure?
items.correct: Distilled water, which contains only the compound H2O
items.misconception: Sea water, because it is clear and colourless
items.why: Everyday language uses clear and clean as synonyms for pure, and dissolved substances are invisible, so the eye gives no evidence either way. Appearance is not evidence of purity. Use melting point or boiling point data, or chromatography, to find out how many substances are really there.
items.random_wrong: Spring water bottled with nothing added at all

items.q: A student says carbon dioxide must be a mixture because it contains two different elements. Why is the student wrong?
items.correct: Its atoms are chemically bonded in fixed proportions
items.misconception: It is a colourless gas, and colourless gases are pure
items.why: Everyday language uses clear and clean as synonyms for pure, and dissolved substances are invisible, so the eye gives no evidence either way. Appearance is not evidence of purity. Use melting point or boiling point data, or chromatography, to find out how many substances are really there.
items.random_wrong: Carbon and oxygen are pure, so this gas is pure

items.q: Which observation is the best evidence that a solid sample is pure?
items.correct: It melts sharply at one specific temperature
items.misconception: It melts gradually over a range of several degrees
items.why: In the lab even pure samples take time to melt, so students read the time taken as a temperature range and stop treating a sharp melting point as the test. Watch the thermometer, not the clock. Pure elements and compounds melt and boil at specific temperatures, so a spread of several degrees means more than one substance is present.
items.random_wrong: It is a fine white powder with no visible specks

items.q: A sample of sea water starts to boil at 102 °C and the temperature keeps rising while it boils. What does this show?
items.correct: It is a mixture, not a pure substance
items.misconception: Salt gives the water a new fixed boiling point
items.why: The single quoted value for salt water in textbooks hides the range, and students remember only that salt raises the boiling point. Look for a steady temperature during boiling. A rising temperature while a liquid boils is the signature of a mixture, whatever the starting value was.
items.random_wrong: The water in it is a different compound

items.q: A carton of milk is labelled pure milk. What does the word pure mean on that label?
items.correct: Nothing has been added to it, so it is in its natural state
items.misconception: It holds only one compound, so it is chemically pure
items.why: The specification's own point is that the two meanings differ. Advertising uses pure to mean unadulterated and natural, and students meet that use thousands of times before they meet the chemical definition once. Ask what is in the sample, not what has been done to it. Chemically pure means one element or one compound and nothing else, so orange juice is a mixture whatever the carton claims.
items.random_wrong: It has been filtered until only water and fat are left

items.q: Pure aspirin melts at 135 °C. A student's prepared sample melts between 122 °C and 128 °C. What do the data show?
items.correct: It is impure: the impurity lowered and spread the melting point
items.misconception: It is pure aspirin, since the average is close to the book value
items.why: Students are used to accepting measurements within experimental error, and averaging a range into a single number throws away the very evidence the range carries. Judge two things: how far the value sits from the data book value, and whether the change happened at one temperature or over a range. A range is decisive on its own.
items.random_wrong: It is pure, because pure solids melt over a range of degrees

items.q: Four liquids were heated to boiling. Which behaviour identifies a pure liquid?
items.correct: It boils steadily at 78 °C until it has all gone
items.misconception: It boils at 100 °C and leaves a white solid behind
items.why: Everyday language uses clear and clean as synonyms for pure, and dissolved substances are invisible, so the eye gives no evidence either way. Appearance is not evidence of purity. Use melting point or boiling point data, or chromatography, to find out how many substances are really there.
items.random_wrong: It boils away over a range from 78 °C to 91 °C

items.q: Which of these is the definition of a formulation?
items.correct: A mixture designed as a useful product
items.misconception: Any mixture containing two or more substances
items.why: Students latch onto the first half of the definition and drop the qualifier that a formulation is designed as a useful product with its components in measured quantities. Apply the whole definition. Ask whether someone chose the components, measured them out and made the product for a purpose. Sea water fails that test; a paint or a fertiliser passes it.
items.random_wrong: A compound made by mixing elements together

items.q: Why are the components of a formulation mixed in carefully measured quantities?
items.correct: So the product has exactly the properties it was designed to have
items.misconception: So the mixture becomes one pure compound as it is stirred
items.why: Students treat purity as a property that each component carries and that survives mixing, rather than as a count of how many substances are present. Count the substances. One element or one compound is pure; two or more not chemically combined is a mixture, no matter how pure each one was on its own.
items.random_wrong: So the components all react and leave no waste behind

items.q: A student is given information about four substances. Which one is a formulation?
items.correct: A paint with pigment, binder and solvent in fixed amounts
items.misconception: Sea water, a mixture of water and many different dissolved salts
items.why: Students latch onto the first half of the definition and drop the qualifier that a formulation is designed as a useful product with its components in measured quantities. Apply the whole definition. Ask whether someone chose the components, measured them out and made the product for a purpose. Sea water fails that test; a paint or a fertiliser passes it.
items.random_wrong: Distilled water sold in bottles for topping up an iron

items.q: A jeweller melts 75% gold with measured amounts of copper and silver to make a harder gold alloy. Is the alloy a formulation?
items.correct: Yes: measured amounts are mixed to give a useful product
items.misconception: No, because a formulation has to be a liquid such as a paint
items.why: The examples students meet first are usually liquids in bottles with ingredient lists, so the state of matter gets bundled into the definition. State of matter is irrelevant. What matters is that the components were mixed in measured quantities to make a useful product.
items.random_wrong: No, because metals are elements, so alloys are pure

items.q: In paper chromatography, which phase is stationary and which is mobile?
items.correct: Paper stationary, solvent mobile
items.misconception: Solvent stationary, the dyes are mobile
items.why: The spots are what students watch, so movement gets identified with them, and it is easy to assume that dissolving is all that matters. The two phases are the paper and the solvent. The dyes are the sample, and each one is shared between the phases to a different extent, which is why they end up at different heights.
items.random_wrong: Paper stationary, the ink is mobile

items.q: Why do the substances in a mixture end up at different heights on a chromatogram?
items.correct: They are distributed differently between the paper and the solvent
items.misconception: Heavier substances are pulled back down the paper by gravity
items.why: Gravity is the everyday explanation for anything that fails to rise, and students have no other model to hand for why a spot stopped where it did. Explain the height by attraction: a substance held strongly by the paper moves a short way, and one that stays dissolved in the moving solvent moves far.
items.random_wrong: The smallest particles fit through the gaps in the paper first

items.q: What does the Rf value of a compound compare?
items.correct: How far the compound moved against how far the solvent moved
items.misconception: The distance the spot moved up the paper, in centimetres
items.why: Both measurements that go into it are in centimetres, and students are rightly drilled to attach units to every answer. Dividing cm by cm leaves a bare number. Write the Rf value as a number alone, with no unit after it.
items.random_wrong: How far the spot moved against the length of the paper

items.q: Which equation gives the Rf value of a substance?
items.correct: Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent
items.misconception: Rf = distance moved by substance x distance moved up by solvent
items.why: If the fraction has been inverted, or the distances combined some other way, the answer comes out above 1 and there is no unit to look wrong, so nothing signals the error. Use Rf below 1 as a check on your own arithmetic. An answer above 1 means the two distances have been combined the wrong way round.
items.random_wrong: Rf = distance moved by substance / total length of paper

items.q: A sample is run in three different solvents and gives one spot each time. What does this show?
items.correct: The sample is a pure compound
items.misconception: The sample must be a single element
items.why: The word mixture is heard as containing different things, and the chemical bonding that separates a compound from a mixture is invisible in a formula such as CO2. A pure substance is a single element or a single compound. In a compound the elements are chemically bonded in fixed proportions and cannot be separated by filtering or evaporating.
items.random_wrong: The spots have simply overlapped

items.q: Two dyes give the same Rf value in one solvent. What should the student do next?
items.correct: Run them again in a different solvent and compare
items.misconception: Conclude that the dyes are the same compound
items.why: Rf is presented as a way of identifying compounds, so a match reads as an identification rather than as evidence that still has to be confirmed. Treat one matching Rf value as consistent with, not proof of, being the same compound. Confirm it by running both again in a different solvent.
items.random_wrong: Repeat the run in the same solvent for longer

items.q: A dye is held strongly by the paper and dissolves only slightly in the solvent. On the chromatogram this dye will
items.correct: move only a short way up, giving a low Rf value
items.misconception: travel with the solvent front, as dissolved dyes do
items.why: The spots are what students watch, so movement gets identified with them, and it is easy to assume that dissolving is all that matters. The two phases are the paper and the solvent. The dyes are the sample, and each one is shared between the phases to a different extent, which is why they end up at different heights.
items.random_wrong: stay on the line, unable to enter the paper

items.q: A chromatogram is run on a food colouring. Which result shows that the colouring is impure?
items.correct: The colouring separates into more than one spot
items.misconception: It gives a single spot, proving it is pure
items.why: One spot looks like a complete result, and students do not expect two substances to happen to travel the same distance. Two compounds can have very similar Rf values in one solvent and separate clearly in another. Only a single spot in every solvent tried supports purity.
items.random_wrong: Its spot is bigger than the spot of the reference dye

items.q: When finding an Rf value from a chromatogram, how is the distance moved by the substance measured?
items.correct: From the pencil line to the spot's centre
items.misconception: From the bottom edge of the paper to the spot
items.why: The solvent really does begin at the bottom of the sheet, so measuring from there feels more honest than measuring from a drawn line. Use the same starting line for both measurements. Measuring from the paper's edge adds an extra centimetre or two to each distance and changes the Rf value.
items.random_wrong: From the pencil line to the top of the spot

items.q: On a chromatogram a spot has moved 3.6 cm from the pencil line and the solvent has moved 9.0 cm. What is the Rf value of the spot?
items.correct: 0.40, worked out as 3.6 cm / 9.0 cm
items.misconception: 5.4 cm, the difference of the two
items.why: If the fraction has been inverted, or the distances combined some other way, the answer comes out above 1 and there is no unit to look wrong, so nothing signals the error. Use Rf below 1 as a check on your own arithmetic. An answer above 1 means the two distances have been combined the wrong way round.
items.random_wrong: 2.5, worked out as 9.0 cm / 3.6 cm

items.q: A spot moved 2.7 cm and the solvent moved 5.9 cm. The calculator shows 0.457627 for the Rf value. How should the answer be given?
items.correct: 0.46, matching the two significant figures measured
items.misconception: 0.4576, since the extra digits make it more accurate
items.why: More digits look more precise, and students are reluctant to throw away figures the calculator has supplied. An answer cannot be more precise than the measurements behind it. Two-significant-figure distances give a two-significant-figure Rf value.
items.random_wrong: 0.457627, exactly as the calculator displays it

items.q: In Required practical 6, why is the start line on the chromatography paper drawn in pencil?
items.correct: Pencil does not dissolve and move up the paper
items.misconception: Ink would react with the solvent to make a new dye
items.why: Students learn the rule as a piece of exam ritual without the reason, then invent a plausible one such as visibility or a reaction. The reason is solubility, not visibility or reactivity. Ink is itself a mixture of dyes that would dissolve and separate, adding spots of its own to the paper.
items.random_wrong: Pencil is easier to see against the coloured dyes

items.q: Why must the solvent in the beaker start below the pencil line on the paper?
items.correct: Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent
items.misconception: Otherwise the solvent front would end up uneven
items.why: The rule is easy to break when the beaker is filled first, and the failure looks like a poor result rather than a broken method. Set the depth so that the solvent starts below the spots. It then rises through them and carries them up the paper, which is the whole point of the run.
items.random_wrong: Otherwise the paper would sink to the beaker's base

items.q: Pure aspirin melts at 135 °C. A sample melts from 122 °C to 128 °C. What has the impurity done?
items.correct: It has lowered the melting point and spread it over a range.
items.misconception: Impurities always raise the melting point, because there is now more material that has to melt.
items.why: Students transfer the salt-and-water boiling result, where the boiling point rises, straight across to melting, and adding something feels as though it should make melting harder. Learn the two effects separately: an impurity lowers a melting point and raises a boiling point, and in both cases spreads the change over a range instead of one temperature.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an alloy a formulation?
items.correct: Yes. An alloy is a mixture of metals blended in measured proportions to give properties such as extra hardness, and the specification lists alloys as formulations.
items.misconception: Alloys cannot be formulations because metals are elements, so an alloy is a pure metal.
items.why: Alloys look like a single shiny metal with no visible components, and students met them as materials rather than as mixtures. An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements. Because the amounts are chosen and measured to give the properties wanted, it fits the definition of a formulation exactly.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Distilled water is sold as a useful product for steam irons. Is it a formulation?
items.correct: No. It is a single compound, and a formulation must be a mixture of components that each do a job.
items.misconception: Anything manufactured and sold as a useful product counts as a formulation.
items.why: Students remember the words useful product from the definition and treat being on sale as the whole test. Check for a mixture first. If the product is one element or one compound it cannot be a formulation, however carefully it was made or however useful it is.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does it matter how much of each component goes into a formulation?
items.correct: Yes. The components are mixed in carefully measured quantities so that the product has the properties it needs.
items.misconception: Only the list of ingredients matters; the proportions can be varied freely.
items.why: Recipes at home tolerate rough quantities, and ingredient lists on packaging give names without amounts, so the measuring is invisible. The proportions are part of the design. Change them and the paint runs, the fuel misfires or the medicine gives the wrong dose, so the product no longer has the required properties.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In paper chromatography, which is the stationary phase and which is the mobile phase?
items.correct: The paper is the stationary phase and the solvent is the mobile phase.
items.misconception: The paper is the mobile phase, because the solvent sits still in the beaker while the paper does the work.
items.why: Students watch the paper being the active piece of apparatus and see a beaker of solvent standing still, so the labels get attached to the wrong objects. Ask what physically moves during the run. The solvent travels up the paper, so the solvent is mobile and the paper, which never moves, is stationary.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the substances separate because the paper acts as a sieve?
items.correct: No. Separation depends on the distribution of each substance between the paper and the solvent.
items.misconception: The paper has tiny holes, so small particles pass through it quickly and large ones are trapped near the start line.
items.why: Filtration is the separation method students meet first, and paper is used there as a sieve, so the mechanism is carried across to chromatography. Nothing passes through the paper in chromatography; the solvent moves along it. How far a substance goes depends on how strongly it is attracted to the paper compared with the solvent.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A spot moved 3.6 cm and the solvent moved 9.0 cm. Is the Rf value 9.0 / 3.6?
items.correct: No. R_f= (distance moved by substance) / (distance moved by solvent), so it is 3.6 / 9.0 = 0.40.
items.misconception: Rf is the solvent distance divided by the substance distance, so the bigger number goes on top.
items.why: Students recall that Rf compares two distances but not which way round, and dividing the larger by the smaller feels like the natural thing to do. The solvent always travels furthest, so it belongs on the bottom of the fraction. Put the substance distance on top and every Rf value comes out less than 1.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a compound have one fixed Rf value?
items.correct: No. Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents, so an Rf value only means something alongside the solvent used.
items.misconception: Rf is a constant for a substance, like its melting point, so it can be looked up whatever the solvent.
items.why: Rf values are given in tables that look like data book constants, and the solvent is often left out of the question. Always record the solvent with the Rf value. Comparing a sample with a reference is only valid when both were run in the same solvent on the same paper.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which part of a spot do you measure to?
items.correct: The centre of the spot, measured from the pencil line where the sample was placed.
items.misconception: Measure to the top edge of the spot, since that is as far as the substance reached.
items.why: Spots spread as they travel, and the leading edge is easier to see than the middle, so it becomes the obvious thing to measure. The specification defines the distance as the centre of the spot from the origin. Measuring to an edge inflates the Rf value and gives a different answer for the same spot.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the bottom of the Rf fraction the length of the paper?
items.correct: No. It is the distance moved by the solvent, measured from the origin to the solvent front.
items.misconception: Divide by the height of the paper, because that is how far the spot could have gone.
items.why: The paper is the obvious fixed length in front of the student, and the solvent front is only a faint pencil mark that is easy to ignore. Mark the solvent front in pencil as soon as the paper comes out, and measure to that line. The solvent almost never reaches the top of the paper.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.8.1 Purity, formulations and chromatography
